title: Hard exam 1
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: quoting, ownership checks, links that dangle, exit statuses and scripts that run with missing arguments.

options.why: Inside single quotes the backslash is not special, so `\$v` stays as typed: the second word is `$v=\$v`.

Word 1: the backslash escapes the first `$` inside double quotes, the second one expands. Word 2: single quotes keep everything literally, backslash included. Word 3: `\$` is a literal `$` and `$v` expands.
The escaped `\$v` is never expanded: it prints a literal `$v`.
The last word is not quoted at all, so its second `$v` is expanded to 5.

questions.title: Reading who
questions.text:
`who` prints these four lines for the same user:
```
ana  tty2   10:01
ana  :0     10:02
ana  pts/0  10:15 (:0)
ana  pts/1  10:40 (10.0.0.7)
```
Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `:0` is a text-mode virtual console, while `tty2` is the graphical session of the user.
options.why: Swapped: `ttyN` is a text virtual console and `:0` is the graphical interface.

options.t: `pts/0` and `pts/1` are text virtual consoles of the machine, reached with Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F6.
options.why: Those are the `ttyN` ones; `pts/N` are text terminals opened inside something else.

options.t: `pts/0` is a terminal window inside the graphical session `:0`; `pts/1` is a text session coming from 10.0.0.7.
options.why: The text in parentheses says where the session came from: the display `:0`, or the remote address (for example over ssh).

options.t: The four lines belong to four different machines, because each session has its own terminal name.
options.why: They are four sessions of the same user on this machine; only the last one comes from another machine.

questions.title: Owner bits only
questions.text: `tool.sh` (a correct bash script) is owned by user `ana` and group `dev`, and ana is a member of `dev`. Its mode is `---r-xr-x`. ana runs `bash tool.sh` and then `./tool.sh`. What happens?

options.t: Both work, because ana is also covered by the group and "others" bits, which allow `r` and `x`.
options.why: The shell stops at the first class that applies: ana is the owner, so only the owner bits count.

options.t: `bash tool.sh` works because only `r` is needed, and `./tool.sh` fails because ana has no `x`.
options.why: Both fail: the owner class has neither `r` nor `x`, and `bash` needs `r` to read the file.

options.t: Both fail with `Permission denied`: ana is judged only by the owner bits, which are `---`.
options.why: The class that matches the user is the only one consulted, so the more generous group and other bits do not help the owner.

options.t: `bash tool.sh` fails but `./tool.sh` works, because the group bits give ana `r-x`.
options.why: `./tool.sh` fails too: the owner bits apply to ana, not the group bits.

questions.title: Writing through a broken link
questions.text:
In an empty directory:
```
echo hi > a
ln -s a b
rm a
echo new > b
```
Which statement is TRUE afterwards?

options.t: `echo new > b` fails with "No such file or directory", because `b` points to a file that does not exist.
options.why: Opening a symbolic link for writing follows it, and `>` creates the missing target.

options.t: `b` is replaced by a regular file with the text `new`, and the link disappears.
options.why: The link is kept: the redirection opens the file it points to, it does not replace the link.

options.t: A new file `a` containing `new` exists, and `b` is a valid link to it again.
options.why: The write follows the link and creates `a`; `cat b` and `cat a` both print `new`.

options.t: `a` is re-created containing `hi`, since the link remembers the old content.
options.why: A symbolic link stores only the path `a`, never the data of the file.

questions.title: Comparing byte by byte
questions.text: `f1` contains the lines `one` and `two`, and `f2` contains `one` and `Two` (both end with a newline). What does `cmp f1 f2` print?

options.t: `f1 f2 differ: byte 4, line 2`
options.why: The first line has 4 bytes (`one` plus the newline), so the first byte of line 2 is number 5; bytes are counted from 1.

options.t: `f1 f2 differ: byte 5, line 1`
options.why: Byte 5 is in the second line: the first line is `one` plus its newline, 4 bytes.

options.t: `2c2` followed by the two lines
options.why: That is the style of `diff`; `cmp` prints one line and stops at the first difference.

options.t: `f1 f2 differ: byte 5, line 2`
options.why: Bytes `o`,`n`,`e`,newline are 1 to 4; `t` against `T` is byte 5, on line 2.

questions.title: Who is the parent
questions.text: From a shell with PID 2215 you run `sleep 100 & sleep 200 & pstree -p`, and in the tree the shell appears as `sshd(2210)───bash(2215)`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `pstree` is the parent of both `sleep` processes, because it is the one that shows them.
options.why: `pstree` only reads the process table; it does not create the other processes.

options.t: Both `sleep` processes and `pstree` itself are children of the shell, bash(2215).
options.why: Each command launched from the prompt, in the background or not, is a child of the shell; `pstree` shows itself as one of them.

options.t: The two `sleep` processes are children of PID 1, since background processes are detached from the shell.
options.why: A background job is still a child of the shell that started it; only an orphan is adopted by PID 1.

options.t: `bash(2215)` is a direct child of PID 1, because the tree always starts at PID 1.
options.why: The tree starts at PID 1, but here the shell hangs below `sshd(2210)`, which is its parent.

questions.title: Count 0, status 1
questions.text: `g` is a file with two lines, `x` and `y`. What do `grep -c zzz g; echo $?` print?

options.t: `0` and then `0`, because the count is 0 and nothing went wrong.
options.why: `$?` is the exit status of `grep`, not its output; `grep` exits with 1 when no line is selected.

options.t: `0` and then `1`
options.why: `-c` prints the number of matching lines (0), and the exit status is 1 because no line matched.

options.t: `1` and then `1`
options.why: The count is the number of matching lines, 0.

options.t: `0` and then `2`, since 2 is the number of lines of the file.
options.why: The exit status is not a line count: 0 means a match, 1 no match and 2 an error.

questions.title: Names and inodes
questions.text: In an empty directory you run `touch a`, `mv a b`, `cp b c`, `ln b d` and `ln -s b e`, and then `ls -i b c d e`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: `b` and `c` show the same inode number, because `c` is a copy with the same content.
options.why: A copy is a new file: it gets its own inode.

options.t: `b` and `e` show the same inode number, because a symbolic link is another name of the same file.
options.why: A symbolic link is a file of its own that holds a path, so it has its own inode.

options.t: `b` has a new inode number because `mv` changed its name from `a`.
options.why: Within one filesystem `mv` only changes the directory entry; the inode stays.

options.t: `b` and `d` show the same inode number, while `c` and `e` each have their own.
options.why: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode.

questions.title: systemctl comments
questions.text: Which of these lines has a comment that does NOT describe what the command does?

options.t: `systemctl get-default   # prints the target the system reaches at boot`
options.why: True: it shows the default target.

options.t: `systemctl isolate rescue.target   # stops the units of the current target and starts those of single-user mode`
options.why: True: it changes the level, like the old runlevel 1.

options.t: `systemctl enable cups   # starts the service now and also at every boot`
options.why: `enable` only registers the service for the next boots; `systemctl start cups` is what starts it now.

options.t: `systemctl disable cups   # removes the service from the boot, without stopping a running instance`
options.why: True: it only changes what starts at boot.

questions.title: Script without an argument
questions.text:
`t.sh` contains:
```
n=$1
if [ $n -lt 0 ]; then echo neg
elif [ $n -eq 0 ]; then echo zero
else echo pos
fi
```
You run `bash t.sh` with no arguments. What happens?
questions.note: Quoting the variable (`[ "$n" -lt 0 ]`) would still fail with "integer expression expected", so check `$#` first.

options.t: It prints `zero`, because an empty value counts as 0.
options.why: `$n` is empty, so each test is `[ -eq 0 ]`: a syntax error, not a comparison with 0.

options.t: It stops at the first test and prints only an error, because a failing test ends the script.
options.why: A failed `[` just returns a non-zero status; the script goes on with the next branch.

options.t: It prints two `unary operator expected` errors on stderr and then `pos` on stdout.
options.why: Both tests are malformed, so both return non-zero and the `else` branch runs.

options.t: It prints `neg`, because the first test `[ -lt 0 ]` is true for an empty value.
options.why: The unquoted empty `$n` vanishes, leaving `[ -lt 0 ]`, which is an error and not "true".
